Content:
In general, the limit of a function [MATH: f(x)] at a point only exists if both the left-sided and right-sided limits exist and are the same.

Content:
For example, suppose we want to compute [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)] for the function whose graph is shown below. To do this, we must first compute the left and right-sided limits.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5633c1581be3cf554a210e0e5736d611]

Content:
As [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 2] from the left, [MATH: y] approaches [MATH: 0.] However, as [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 2] from the right, [MATH: y] approaches [MATH: 1.] Therefore, we have the following left and right-sided limits.

Content:
[MATH: Left-sided limit:|lim_(x → 2^{−})f(x) = 0; Right-sided limit:|lim_(x → 2^{+})f(x) = 1]

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)=\text{DNE}]

  • Statement II is true. When approaching [MATH: x=1] from the left and from the right, we get [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1^-}f(x)=0, \qquad \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1^+}f(x)=3,] respectively. We cannot say that the limits are equal because we can't compare the undefined values.

In conclusion, only statements I and II are true.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In general, the limit of a function [MATH: f(x)] at a point only exists if both the left-sided and right-sided limits exist and are the same.

Content:
For example, suppose we want to compute [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)] for the function whose graph is shown below. To do this, we must first compute the left and right-sided limits.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5633c1581be3cf554a210e0e5736d611]

Content:
As [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 2] from the left, [MATH: y] approaches [MATH: 0.] However, as [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 2] from the right, [MATH: y] approaches [MATH: 1.] Therefore, we have the following left and right-sided limits.

Content:
[MATH: Left-sided limit:|lim_(x → 2^{−})f(x) = 0; Right-sided limit:|lim_(x → 2^{+})f(x) = 1]

Content:
Both of these limits exist. However, they are not the same. Consequently, the overall limit at [MATH: x=2] does not exist:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)=\text{DNE}]

---

[IMG: /graphics/c8b132237879e9590da52da233c11da9]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
From the graph, we see that as we approach [MATH: x=0] from the left, the [MATH: y] value approaches [MATH: 2.] So the left-hand limit is
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0^{-}}f(x)=2.]

Similarly, when we approach [MATH: x=0] from the right, the [MATH: y] value again approaches [MATH: 2.] So the right-hand limit is
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0^{+}}f(x)=2.]

Since both the left and right-hand limits exist and are equal to [MATH: 2,] we conclude that
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=2.]
